title: X Feed Digest
summary: Google I/O aftershocks dominated the feed: the real story is Google repositioning Antigravity as a shared agent platform across desktop, CLI, SDK, managed runtimes, and Android rather than shipping yet another AI IDE.

Pricing and capacity became explicit strategy. OpenAI is now selling 1-3 year compute commitments, while Google cut AI Ultra pricing and expanded bundles/limits—only to trigger immediate backlash from early adopters who bought the day before the change.

The most useful workflow posts were practical, not flashy: official managed-agent infrastructure, steadier Codex CLI ergonomics, and a strong push toward HTML-based plans/prototypes for agent collaboration instead of giant Markdown files.

Speed and deployability are emerging as enterprise differentiators. Cerebras is selling frontier inference throughput, while research shared in the feed argued readable LLM-written control code can beat heavier black-box approaches in some real engineering tasks.

Human verification is still the bottleneck. Linux maintainers are already drowning in AI-generated bug spam, and even strong models still need cross-checking in high-stakes domains like medical interpretation.

items.title: @mark_k: Antigravity Becomes the Product
items.body: Mark's sharpest read on Google I/O was that Antigravity 2.0 no longer feels like an IDE with agents bolted on. The real product is now the shared agent layer—desktop app, CLI, SDK, managed agents, scheduled tasks, and subagents all pointing to one cross-surface runtime.

items.title: @geminicli: Gemini CLI Users Are Being Moved to Antigravity CLI
items.body: Google said consumer Gemini CLI users are being migrated to the new Go-based Antigravity CLI, which emphasizes asynchronous multi-agent workflows and a unified backend. The practical deadline matters: free, Pro, and Ultra consumer access stops being served on June 18, while enterprise usage stays supported.

items.title: @Google: Managed Agents Land in the Gemini API
items.body: Google is packaging the same Antigravity harness it uses internally behind a single API call, complete with a hosted Linux environment. That's a meaningful shift from model access toward selling a full agent runtime as infrastructure.

items.title: @CodexReleases: Codex CLI Gets Better Auth and Structured Resume
items.body: Codex CLI 0.132.0 adds first-class authentication flows in the Python SDK, richer run metadata, and `codex exec resume --output-schema` for enforcing structured JSON without losing session context. It's the kind of operational polish that makes automation chains easier to trust and reuse.

items.title: @FakeMaidenMaker: HTML Is Emerging as an Agent Workspace
items.body: A widely shared summary of Anthropic's new guidance argued that Claude Code teams are replacing long Markdown plans with HTML files, prototypes, and mini-editors. The useful idea is not HTML for HTML's sake but using richer, more readable artifacts that humans will actually open and iterate on with the agent.

items.title: @OpenAI: Guaranteed Capacity Goes Commercial
items.body: OpenAI introduced Guaranteed Capacity, letting customers make 1-3 year commitments for discounted tokens and assured access to compute across its product portfolio. The larger signal is that frontier demand remains constrained enough for compute reservations to become a product category.

items.title: @GeminiApp: Google Reprices AI Ultra
items.body: Google cut its top AI Ultra plan from $250 to $200 per month and added a new $100 tier while expanding usage limits and bundled perks. That looks less like a simple promo and more like active competitive pressure in premium consumer AI packaging.

items.title: @bridgemindai: Repricing Backlash Hit Immediately
items.body: One of the more useful counter-signals came from an Ultra subscriber who paid full price the day before Google cut the plan and said there was no refund or credit. Even if the product roadmap is improving, abrupt repricing can destroy trust with exactly the users most likely to test and evangelize new models.

items.title: @cerebras: Inference Speed Is Now a Frontline Sales Pitch
items.body: Cerebras said Kimi K2.6 is running in enterprise trials at roughly 1,000 tokens per second, framing throughput itself as the headline. That matters because enterprise buyers are starting to evaluate model vendors not just on quality, but on whether latency and cost make agentic workflows usable at scale.

items.title: @sama: OpenAI Offered YC Startups $2M in Tokens
items.body: Sam Altman said OpenAI offered to invest $2 million in tokens into every company in the current YC batch. The strategic read is that labs are no longer just selling API access—they're subsidizing an ecosystem of startups whose products and internal habits will be built around their models from day one.

items.title: @MaxForAI: Linus Draws a Line on AI Bug Spam
items.body: A translated thread on the Linux security mailing list captured the real failure mode of AI-assisted bug hunting: unvalidated, duplicated reports dumped onto maintainers. The durable lesson is that AI can widen search, but humans still have to verify impact, threat model, and fixes before shipping the work downstream.

items.title: @manateelazycat: Medical Use Still Demands Cross-Checking
items.body: A concrete anecdote about conflicting model interpretations of a blood test was a good reminder that confidence is not reliability, especially in health contexts. The useful habit here is simple: cross-check with other sources and defer to clinicians rather than treating one model answer as diagnosis.

items.title: @PANews: A Monet Mistaken for AI
items.body: An artist reportedly posted a cropped Monet, labeled it as AI-generated, and watched critics attack its lack of soul before revealing the trick and selling the backlash as an NFT. The sharper takeaway is epistemic: once people see an AI label, many stop looking and start performing certainty.

items.title: @0xLogicrw: Readable Code Beats Black-Box Control
items.body: One of the most interesting research shares claimed Codex 5.5 wrote short, interpretable control rules for fluid-dynamics tasks that outperformed both Gemini 3 Pro, Claude Opus 4.7, and strong reinforcement-learning baselines in many scenarios. Even if the result needs broader replication, it's a compelling signal that human-readable code agents may be more robust than brittle trained controllers in some engineering loops.
